strengths: VisuRiddles addresses an important weakness of MLLMs through diverse abstract visual tasks, combining curated examination questions with RAVEN and Sudoku. The described annotation and review process is a useful foundation.
PRS provides a potentially valuable source of scalable supervision: 80K synthetic examples spanning 34 sub-rules, with aligned visual descriptions.
The evaluation covers numerous open and proprietary models. Reported improvements are substantial, particularly from 14% to 95% on RAVEN and 0% to 60% on Sudoku.
The visual-versus-description experiments provide evidence that input representation and perceptual access materially affect performance.
weaknesses: The central attribution to perception is not established. Fine-tuning changes both perceptual and reasoning capabilities; unchanged architecture does not isolate the source of improvement. Table 5 varies dataset size but lacks matched answer-only, reasoning-only, and perceptual-supervision controls.

The bottleneck experiment uses an unspecified subset of deliberately tractable synthetic problems rather than VisuRiddles itself. Full descriptions and checks excluding rule or answer information are absent, despite generated annotations including reasoning traces. Furthermore, description-based RAVEN accuracy remains only 25–35%, indicating substantial residual reasoning limitations.

Aggregate scores are inconsistent with the reported category results. In Table 3, PRS's 43.7% matches the unweighted category mean, whereas the baseline's 20.9% does not; using Table 1 counts gives approximately 40.9% and 21.0%, respectively. Table 5's 60K result reports 37.2%, versus approximately 40.7% macro-average or 38.2% sample-weighted accuracy. These discrepancies undermine headline comparisons.

Generalization is insufficiently tested. The largest gains occur on generated RAVEN and Sudoku tasks, but generator separation, duplicate checks, and held-out rules or templates are not documented. There is no external benchmark evaluation, and only one model is fine-tuned. The claim of outperforming other models across all categories contradicts Table 3, including numerical reasoning, attributes, and Other.

Reproducibility is limited by missing training duration, trainable components, exact supervision format, evaluation prompts, decoding budgets, image preprocessing, and scoring procedures. The statement that all models use vLLM does not explain proprietary API evaluation. No uncertainty estimates or repeated training runs are reported.

Benchmark validation and positioning need strengthening. Human accuracy lacks participant counts and a clear measurement protocol, preventing a controlled human–model comparison. The manuscript does not sufficiently demonstrate added coverage relative to existing AVR benchmarks or distinguish PRS from prior procedural generation and structured-supervision methods.

strengths: VisuRiddles targets a relevant limitation of multimodal models, combining exam-derived visual puzzles with RAVEN and Sudoku across explicitly defined reasoning categories.
PRS offers a potentially useful source of synthetic puzzles with aligned perceptual annotations. The reported improvements on RAVEN (14% to 95%) and Sudoku (0% to 60%) are substantial.
The evaluation includes a broad selection of open and proprietary models. The image-versus-description experiments provide useful evidence that visual representation affects task performance.
weaknesses: The central claim that perception is the primary bottleneck is not established. Table 4 evaluates an unspecified subset of deliberately tractable synthetic tasks, rather than the main benchmark. Structured descriptions also simplify representation and may supply task-relevant abstractions. Significant failures remain with descriptions, including GPT-4o achieving only 15% on Sudoku and 25% on RAVEN. These results demonstrate a perceptual contribution, but do not establish that reasoning is adequate.

The training experiments do not isolate perceptual supervision. There is no matched comparison using the same synthetic images with answer-only supervision, reasoning-only supervision, or descriptions without reasoning traces. Increasing training-set size in Table 5 cannot distinguish improved perception from task-specific reasoning practice. Keeping architecture and parameter count fixed does not justify attributing all gains to perception.

Reported aggregate scores are inconsistent with the category results. Using Table 1's sample counts, the proposed model's Table 3 accuracy is approximately 40.9%, whereas 43.7% is its unweighted category mean. The baseline's reported 20.9% instead approximately matches its sample-weighted accuracy; its category mean is 20.4%. Table 5's 40K average of 30.9% matches neither the weighted result (32.2%) nor the category mean (33.5%). These discrepancies undermine the headline comparisons and require corrected results with an explicit aggregation rule.

Generalization is insufficiently demonstrated. The largest gains occur on generated RAVEN and Sudoku tasks, but train/test separation by generation seed, template, rule combination, and graphical assets is not documented. There are no external benchmark evaluations or held-out-rule tests. Improvements on the exam-derived categories are smaller, and performance on Other decreases. The claim of outperforming other models across all categories is contradicted by Table 3.

Benchmark validation and the human comparison are incomplete. Section 3.1 reports 770 basic samples, while Table 1 lists 800. Human scores are attributed to Fenbi without participant counts, testing conditions, uncertainty, or a clear account of comparability with model evaluation. Public exam sourcing also warrants a contamination analysis, and annotation agreement is not quantified.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript omits exact evaluation prompts, decoding and reasoning budgets, image preprocessing, training duration, trainable components, and the precise supervision format. The statement that all models use vLLM does not explain proprietary-model evaluation. The synthetic diagnostic subset size and statistical uncertainty are missing, and the promised release location is blank.

Novelty is insufficiently distinguished from existing AVR generators, perception-versus-reasoning diagnostics, and cross-modal formalization methods. The related-work discussion lists relevant approaches but provides little concrete comparison establishing what PRS or the benchmark uniquely contributes.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of multimodal models through a benchmark combining five visual reasoning dimensions with RAVEN and Sudoku tasks.
PRS provides a potentially useful resource: 80,000 synthetic examples with structured perceptual annotations spanning 34 sub-rules.

Evaluation covers a broad selection of open and proprietary models. Reported fine-tuning gains are substantial on RAVEN (14% to 95%) and Sudoku (0% to 60%), with improvements across the five core categories.
The visual-versus-textual input experiment provides evidence that access to accurate perceptual descriptions can substantially improve performance.
weaknesses: The central attribution to perceptual supervision is not isolated. There is no matched training comparison using the same synthetic examples with answer-only or conventional reasoning supervision. Increasing annotated training volume cannot distinguish improved perception from task-specific reasoning learning.

The bottleneck experiment uses an unspecified subset of deliberately tractable synthetic tasks rather than VisuRiddles itself. Structured descriptions also change the representation and may supply useful abstractions; their information content is not sufficiently documented to exclude reasoning assistance. These results support a perceptual limitation, but not the stronger claim that reasoning capacity is adequate.

Aggregate results are inconsistent with the reported category scores and dataset sizes. In Table 3, the trained model's scores yield approximately 40.94% when weighted by Table 1 counts, whereas 43.7% matches a macro-average. The baseline's reported 20.9% instead approximately matches its weighted average, while its macro-average is 20.4%. Table 5's 60K result matches neither convention. The claimed overall gains require correction and a precise metric definition.

Generalization evidence is limited to one fine-tuned backbone and one benchmark. The largest gains occur on generated RAVEN and Sudoku tasks, without documented separation by rules, templates, or generation sources. There are no external benchmark results or comparisons against existing synthetic training resources to establish broader value.

The human comparison lacks participant counts, testing conditions, and an explanation of how platform-derived reference answers produce the reported human accuracies. Benchmark documentation also conflicts: the text reports 770 basic examples, while Table 1 lists 800. Public exam provenance is not accompanied by a contamination assessment.

Reproducibility is insufficient: training duration, trainable components, supervision serialization, evaluation prompts, decoding budgets, and the diagnostic subset size are missing. The statement that all models use vLLM does not explain proprietary API evaluation. No uncertainty estimates or repeated training runs are reported.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. The method does not outperform all models in every category, and performance decreases on Other. Claims about interpretability and ineffective inference-time scaling rely on limited qualitative examples and comparisons without controlled inference budgets. Novelty relative to existing AVR generators and perception-to-text approaches is also insufficiently established.

strengths: VisuRiddles addresses a relevant problem with 1,000 examples spanning eight categories, combining examination-derived visual puzzles with RAVEN and Sudoku. The accompanying synthesizer provides useful structured perceptual supervision.
The reported in-benchmark gains are substantial: Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 24.6% to 39.5% after SFT and 46.8% after GRPO, exceeding the strongest evaluated general-purpose models overall.

Table 3 provides meaningful evidence that input representation matters: replacing synthetic images with structured descriptions improves GPT-4o from 27.6% to 60.1% and Qwen2.5-VL-72B from 30.9% to 73.6%.
The paper includes component ablations, numerous model comparisons, qualitative examples, and an external evaluation on VisuLogic.
weaknesses: The central claim that perception is the primary bottleneck is not adequately isolated. Table 3 uses synthetic puzzles deliberately designed to have easier reasoning, and structured descriptions can supply useful abstractions beyond visual recognition. The paper lacks a corresponding controlled study on the real benchmark, direct perception measurements, and a quantitative decomposition of perceptual versus reasoning errors. The evidence supports perception as an important bottleneck, but not its claimed primacy.

The training ablations confound perceptual supervision, reasoning supervision, and task-specific adaptation. The CoT condition itself incorporates structured descriptions; there is no matched reasoning-only SFT condition, answer-only SFT baseline, or Caption-plus-GRPO condition. Consequently, Table 4 does not establish which supervision component explains the gains or substantiate the proposed separation between perceptual SFT and reasoning RL.

Novelty and positioning are insufficiently established. PAVR combines conventional SFT and GRPO with answer and format rewards. Its main potential contribution is therefore the data resource, but the paper does not provide a detailed comparison against closely related benchmarks and synthetic training approaches such as VisuLogic, MARVEL, and VisualSphinx, or controlled comparisons with alternative training datasets.

Generalization evidence is limited. On VisuLogic, PAVR reaches 30.6%, compared with 26.0% for its base model, but remains below the reported 31.1% task-trained InternVL baseline. Only one backbone is trained, and there are no held-out rule or template evaluations, repeated runs, or uncertainty estimates. These results support some transfer, but not the breadth of the paper's claims.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The manuscript omits essential optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch sizes, trainable components, GRPO sampling and KL settings, reward weights, data mixtures, and detailed inference budgets. Appendix C claims all models use vLLM despite including proprietary API models, and its stated model counts do not match its table. The image-versus-description experiment also lacks a clearly specified subset size and selection protocol.

Benchmark validity needs stronger documentation. The paper describes internal duplicate removal but does not establish separation from related examination-derived benchmarks or explain synthetic train/test separation by instances, templates, and rules. Human scores are attributed to an educational platform without participant counts or evaluation conditions. Correct-answer filtering of generated CoT does not validate the reasoning traces themselves. These gaps weaken both the benchmark comparisons and the claimed reliability of the training resource.

strengths: VisuRiddles addresses a relevant weakness of multimodal models through a 1,000-question benchmark and a synthetic generator with aligned perceptual descriptions.
The reported improvements are substantial: Qwen2.5-VL-7B increases from 24.6% to 39.5% after SFT and 46.8% after GRPO, outperforming the evaluated general-purpose models overall.
The visual-versus-description comparisons and caption-only, GRPO-only, and combined-training ablations provide useful evidence that perceptual supervision helps abstract visual reasoning.
weaknesses: The central claim that perception is the primary bottleneck is not adequately isolated. Table 3 uses deliberately easier synthetic problems, and structured descriptions also supply task-relevant abstractions that can simplify reasoning. Appendix B.2 even describes annotations containing reasoning traces. Without auditing this information and measuring perception separately, these results establish the usefulness of structured representations rather than the primacy of perception.

The training ablations confound perception, reasoning supervision, and domain adaptation. The CoT condition includes perceptual descriptions, but there is no matched answer-only SFT or reasoning-trace condition without those descriptions. Caption-plus-GRPO is also missing. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed perception-first mechanism.

Methodological novelty is limited: PAVR combines synthetic supervision, conventional SFT, and standard GRPO with answer and format rewards. The paper does not sufficiently differentiate its resource and training approach from closely related work such as VisuLogic, VisualSphinx, PuzzleVQA, and R1-OneVision through direct, controlled comparisons.

Generalization evidence is modest. On the only external benchmark, VisuLogic, PAVR achieves 30.6%, versus 26.0% for its base model and 31.1% for the reported InternVL2.5-38B-RL baseline. There are no held-out rule, template, or icon experiments, and overlap checks against other civil-service-question benchmarks are not documented.

Reproducibility and evaluation reporting are insufficient. Training omits key optimization and GRPO settings; evaluation omits actual decoding parameters, image-resolution settings, reasoning budgets, and detailed answer parsing. Appendix C's statement that all models use vLLM does not explain proprietary API evaluation. Synthetic diagnostic sample sizes, repeated runs, and uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. PAVR does not outperform every model in every category: o3 scores 40.2% on Style versus PAVR's 39.3%. Prompting comparisons and isolated qualitative examples do not establish that inference-time scaling generally fails. Human scores taken from an educational platform also lack participant counts and comparable testing conditions, weakening the claimed human–model gap.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of multimodal models: interpreting fine-grained visual structure in abstract reasoning tasks.

VisuRiddles combines 1,000 evaluation problems across eight categories with a configurable synthesizer producing aligned perceptual descriptions and reasoning traces. This could be a useful research resource.
The reported improvements are substantial: PAVR increases Qwen2.5-VL-7B accuracy from 24.6% to 46.8%, outperforming the evaluated larger and proprietary models overall.
The description-input experiments and caption/SFT/GRPO ablations provide evidence that perceptual supervision is beneficial and complements reasoning optimization.
weaknesses: The central claim that perception is the primary bottleneck is insufficiently established. Table 3 uses deliberately easier synthetic problems, and structured descriptions supply an oracle representation that can simplify abstraction and reasoning as well as perception. There is no corresponding controlled study on the real benchmark or quantitative measurement of perceptual errors before and after training.

The training ablations do not isolate the proposed mechanism. The CoT condition includes perceptual descriptions, but there is no matched CoT-only condition without descriptions, answer-only SFT baseline, or caption-plus-GRPO condition. Consequently, improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to perceptual supervision rather than task-specific training, reasoning distillation, or training budget.

Methodological novelty is limited: PAVR combines standard SFT and GRPO with correctness and format rewards. The resource contribution needs clearer differentiation from closely related benchmarks and synthetic training approaches, particularly VisuLogic, VisualSphinx, and cross-modal formalization methods.

External validation is modest. On VisuLogic, PAVR improves the reported 7B baseline from 26.0% to 30.6%, but remains below the listed 31.1% RL baseline. This supports some transfer, but provides limited evidence for the broader claims. No held-out-rule or held-out-template evaluation establishes compositional generalization.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are inadequately documented. Learning rates, batch sizes, trainable components, GRPO sampling and KL settings, reward weights, exact prompts, image preprocessing, and generation budgets are missing. Appendix C's claim that all models use vLLM does not explain proprietary API evaluation. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are reported.

Benchmark validation needs more detail: training/test overlap controls, relationships between synthesis rules and evaluation problems, annotation agreement, and source licensing are unspecified. Human scores are attributed to an educational platform without participant counts or a comparable testing protocol, limiting the human-performance claims.
